cards.front: What is the key to sharing Washington roads?
cards.back: Courtesy, respect and awareness of others are the key to sharing Washington roads, and your care could save a life, including your own.

cards.front: Where do pedestrians have the right-of-way?
cards.back: Always yield to pedestrians, who, like bicyclists, hold the right-of-way at every crosswalk and intersection, marked or unmarked.

cards.front: How long must you wait for a crossing pedestrian, and what changes for someone with a cane or service animal?
cards.back: Wait until a pedestrian has cleared your lane plus one more lane before going, but for someone crossing with a wheelchair, a cane, a guide dog or another service animal, stay stopped until the whole street is crossed.
cards.memory_hook: one extra lane, or whole street

cards.front: How does the waiting rule differ for a pedestrian with a mobility aid?
cards.back: A pedestrian without a mobility aid must clear your lane and one more before you go, but a pedestrian with a wheelchair, cane or service animal must reach the far side of the street.

cards.front: Which people should you watch for because they may not see you?
cards.back: Watch for people who cannot see you, are distracted, or may be confused, such as children, road workers, tourists or someone on a phone.

cards.front: Why should you not honk near a service animal?
cards.back: Interfering with a service animal is unlawful, and you should not honk near one because the noise can confuse or frighten the animal or its handler.

cards.front: What do a school bus's red and yellow lights mean?
cards.back: School bus lights work like traffic signals: red means stop, and yellow means use caution and slow down.

cards.front: What happens to the fine for passing a stopped school bus?
cards.back: Passing a stopped school bus doubles the fine, and it is unlawful to pass a bus while its red lights flash.

cards.front: Who must stop for a school bus's flashing red lights?
cards.back: Every driver going the same direction as the bus must stop for flashing red lights and the extended stop sign, including drivers in any turn lane, and a center turn lane may never be used to pass.

cards.front: Can you use a center turn lane to get around a stopped school bus?
cards.back: A center turn lane is not a way around a stopped school bus, because drivers in every turn lane must stop too.

cards.front: When may you move again after stopping for a school bus?
cards.back: You may move again only once the lights stop flashing, the stop sign folds back and the metal arm returns to the front bumper, and you should keep watching for children afterward.
cards.memory_hook: lights off, sign in, arm back

cards.front: On a two-lane road, who stops for a school bus with flashing red lights?
cards.back: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop when the bus's red lights flash and its stop sign is out.

cards.front: On a multilane road, who stops for a school bus, and what conditions does the oncoming exception name?
cards.back: On a multilane road, drivers behind the bus always stop, while the guide's exception for oncoming drivers names two conditions, a road of three or more lanes and lanes split by a median or barrier, without saying whether one alone is enough.

cards.front: On a two-lane road, do oncoming drivers stop for a school bus?
cards.back: On a two-lane road, oncoming drivers stop for a school bus with flashing red lights just like drivers behind it, and they move on only after the lights stop, the sign retracts and the arm returns to the bumper.

cards.front: Whom does the multilane exception help?
cards.back: The multilane exception helps only oncoming traffic; anyone traveling behind the bus on any multilane road must still stop.

cards.front: When must you yield to a transit bus?
cards.back: Yield to a transit bus going your direction that has signaled and is pulling back into traffic.

cards.front: Why should you not ride alongside a large truck for long?
cards.back: Large trucks and buses have blind zones on each side, so do not ride alongside them for long, and if you cannot see the driver's mirrors the driver cannot see you.

cards.front: How much room does a loaded truck need to stop at highway speed?
cards.back: A loaded truck with good brakes at fifty-five miles per hour needs four hundred fifty feet to stop completely, so cutting in front of one without room is dangerous.

cards.front: When is it safe to merge in front of a large vehicle?
cards.back: Before merging in front of a large vehicle, wait until both of its headlights show in your rearview mirror, then keep up with traffic.

cards.front: Is one headlight in your mirror enough before merging ahead of a truck?
cards.back: Before merging ahead of a large vehicle you need both of its headlights in your rearview mirror, not just one, and after merging you keep pace with traffic rather than slowing in front of it.

cards.front: Why should you wait before passing a turning large vehicle?
cards.back: Large vehicles may need more than one lane to turn and two lanes in a roundabout, and passing one while it turns is a frequent cause of crashes, so wait until the turn is done.

cards.front: What should you do near hazardous-materials vehicles and on steep grades?
cards.back: Keep away from vehicles placarded as carrying hazardous materials when you can, and expect slow large vehicles in the right lane on long, steep grades.

cards.front: Why should you not follow a snowplow closely?
cards.back: Snowplows can throw snow up and off the road in a blizzard-like cloud, so do not follow them closely.

cards.front: What rights do motorcyclists have, and why leave extra room?
cards.back: Motorcyclists share the same rights and traffic laws as other drivers, but they are smaller, harder to see and more vulnerable, so leave extra following room, more still on wet or slick roads.

cards.front: Is a motorcycle entitled to a full lane?
cards.back: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane width, so never move into its lane beside it, even if the rider is far to one side.

cards.front: How do you check for motorcycles before a right turn?
cards.back: Motorcycles hide easily in blind zones, so before a right turn look left, right and left again with a shoulder check, and remember drivers often misjudge an oncoming motorcycle's speed.

cards.front: What road hazards can make a rider change speed or lane position?
cards.back: Gravel, debris, pavement seams, potholes and even manhole covers can force a rider to change speed or lane position, so expect those moves.

cards.front: Why stay alert beside a motorcycle's lights?
cards.back: Riders may slow by easing the throttle without showing a brake light, and some motorcycle turn signals do not cancel on their own, so stay alert beside them.

cards.front: Why can't a motorcycle's lights alone tell you its plan?
cards.back: A motorcycle can slow down with no brake light showing, and its turn signal may still blink after the turn, so neither light alone tells you what the rider will do.

cards.front: What rights and duties do bicyclists have, and why are they at high risk?
cards.back: Bicyclists carry the same rights and duties as vehicle drivers, and because bikes are small and hard to see, riders face a high risk of serious injury or death.

cards.front: May a bicyclist use the full lane, and how much space do you leave when following?
cards.back: A bicyclist may legally use the full lane, you may not share a lane with one, and when following a bicyclist you leave at least three feet of space.

cards.front: How is a bicyclist riding in a crosswalk treated?
cards.back: A bicyclist riding in a crosswalk counts as a pedestrian, so you must yield in marked and unmarked crosswalks alike.

cards.front: How is a bicyclist treated on the road versus in a crosswalk?
cards.back: A bicyclist on the road is treated as a vehicle with a right to the full lane, but a bicyclist in a crosswalk is treated as a pedestrian you must yield to.

cards.front: How do you pass a bicyclist safely?
cards.back: To pass a bicyclist, move over a full lane when two lanes run your way, or use the other lane only without oncoming traffic, pass slowly on their left with at least three feet from your widest point, and do not pass just before a right turn.

cards.front: How is the passing gap for a bicyclist measured?
cards.back: The three-foot passing gap for a bicyclist is measured from the widest part of your vehicle, and with one lane each way you use the other lane only when no traffic is coming.

cards.front: What do bike lanes look like, and when may you drive in one?
cards.back: Bike lanes are often green with solid white lines and a bicycle symbol, and you may drive in one only to turn or to cross it to park at the curb.

cards.front: Where may you cross railroad tracks, and what do flashing red lights mean?
cards.back: Cross railroad tracks only at designated crossings, and flashing red lights there mean a train is coming and you must stay outside the gates.

cards.front: Who has the right-of-way at a crossing, and what if the gate is up but lights flash?
cards.back: Trains always have the right-of-way and can need up to a mile to stop, so stop for flashing lights and bells even if the gate is up, and never go around a gate.

cards.front: How far from the nearest rail must you stop?
cards.back: Stop fifteen to fifty feet from the nearest rail when signals flash, a gate is lowering or down, a flagger signals, a train is close or sounds its horn, or a stop sign is posted.

cards.front: What are the limits of the railroad stop zone?
cards.back: The railroad stop zone is no closer than fifteen feet and no farther than fifty feet from the nearest rail, and flashing lights with bells mean stop even when the gate is still up.

cards.front: What do you do if your vehicle stalls at a crossing?
cards.back: Never stop on the tracks, and if your vehicle stalls at a crossing, get everyone out right away, because trains can come from either direction on any track.

cards.front: Whom do you call about something on or near the tracks?
cards.back: If something is on or near the tracks, phone the number shown on the crossing's blue and white Emergency Notification System sign, quote the crossing ID, or dial nine hundred eleven if there is no sign.

cards.front: Which number comes first for a problem on the tracks?
cards.back: A problem on the tracks goes first to the number on the blue and white Emergency Notification System sign, and nine hundred eleven is the fallback only when no sign is posted.

cards.front: How much space do you keep from light rail trains?
cards.back: Near light rail, keep at least one car length between you and the train and never stop or park on the tracks.

cards.front: How do you identify and pass a slow farm vehicle?
cards.back: Farm vehicles built for twenty-five miles per hour or less display a triangle emblem on the back, and passing one calls for patience, a full lane change where possible and at least three feet of clearance.

cards.front: What do you do for an emergency vehicle using lights or sirens?
cards.back: For a fire truck, ambulance or police car using lights or sirens, pull right and stop at once, then signal and rejoin traffic only after it passes, in the order you were in before.

cards.front: When and how do you rejoin traffic after an emergency vehicle passes?
cards.back: For an emergency vehicle you pull to the right and stop as soon as you see or hear it, and you signal and rejoin traffic in your original order only once it has gone by.

recap_hooks.text: Courtesy matters, and pedestrians have the right-of-way at every crosswalk, marked or unmarked.
Wait until they clear your lane plus one, or the whole street with a mobility aid or service animal.
Watch for children, workers and distracted people.
Red bus lights mean stop, passing a stopped bus doubles the fine, and every same-direction lane stops.
Move only when the lights stop, the sign folds and the arm returns.
Two-lane roads stop both ways; multilane exceptions help only oncoming traffic; yield to merging transit buses.
Avoid truck blind zones, and remember a loaded truck needs a long distance to stop.
Merge ahead only with both headlights in your mirror, and let wide turns finish.
Keep away from hazardous loads and do not follow snowplows closely.
Motorcyclists have the same rights, a full lane and need extra room.
Check blind zones twice, expect hazard-driven moves, and do not trust their lights alone.
Bicyclists are vehicles with a right to the full lane, but pedestrians in a crosswalk.
Pass with a full lane where possible and at least three feet from your widest point; enter bike lanes only to turn or park.
Cross only at designated crossings; trains always have the right-of-way.
Stop fifteen to fifty feet from the rail, never on the tracks, and get out if stalled.
Call the sign's number about track problems, and stay a car length from light rail.
Be patient with triangle-marked farm vehicles, and pull right and stop for emergency vehicles, rejoining in order.
